newsitem.title: HONG KONG: INTERVIEW-Volkswagen faces big China challenge.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Volkswagen faces big China challenge.

text.p: Shanghai Volkswagen, China's largest domestic car maker, is facing greater price competition because the government pricing policy forces rivals to sell for little or no profit, Volkswagen's Asia-Pacific unit said.

"In China, the price is very important," said Martin Posth, chairman and president of Volkswagen Asia-Pacific Ltd and a member of the management Board of Volkwagen AG. "And we are not free to make the prices."

The central government's State Price Bureau sets guidelines for the retail prices of all cars, so domestic competitors, including foreign-invested joint ventures, are charging the same price as Volkswagen even though their costs are usually higher, Posth said.
While they may therefore have very thin, or no, profit margins, the pricing policy was threatening Volkswagen's market share, he said in an interview on Thursday.

Nonetheless, the German carmaker's two joint ventures with Shanghai Automotive Industrial Corp in Shanghai and First Automotive Corp (FAW) in Changchun in northern Jilin province are expanding their grip on the China market.
"Up to the end of 1996, sales of Volkswagen and Audi models in China, including some 4,600 imported cars, rose to 239,846 units, compared with 219,431 in 1995," said Posth.
Volkswagen calculates it produced 61.5 percent of all domestically manufactured passenger cars in China.
Shanghai Volkswagen, which produces the Santana, said its sales rose 25.2 percent to 200,015 cars, retaining its place as the nation's leading car maker for the past 10 years.
FAW Volkswagen sold 8,567 Audis and 25,666 Jettas, the latter number a 40.6 percent increase over 1995.
"Total output of all domestic producers rose 21.1 percent in 1996," Posth said by comparison.
But rising industry output is not necessarily something to celebrate, because the market is glutted with cars.
China has 102 automakers, although only five produce more than 100,000 vehicles per year.

The government's wants the industry to consolidate into a few large, well-integrated manufacturers by 2000, grouping the smaller producers with market leaders and closing down smaller, inefficient plants where necessary.
According to the 1994 policy, only those with installed capacity of 150,000 vehicles will make the cut-off, and that is why everybody wants to make cars regardless of the profit margin.
The situation is not likely to get better soon, Posth said.
"What we have today is over-capacity and what we have tomorrow is over-capacity," he said.
Posth said total installed capacity of cars at the end of 1996 was about 600,000 vehicles, while market demand was only 430,000.
The prolonged belt tightening of the past few years as China tried to dampen excessive economic growth has added to the industry's problems, drying up credit and demand.
"Last year was a crisis year for the auto industry in China," said Andreas Meurer, public relations manager for Volkswagen Asia Pacific Ltd.
Sales slumped in the second and third quarters of 1996 and did not pick up until the tail end of the year, he said.
Industry sources add the market is also flooded with legally and illegally imported passengers cars.
To stimulate sales and absorb the production and import glut, the profitable Shanghai joint venture was asked by the government to lower its prices, which it did. Other manufacturers followed suit.
Prices are likely to fall further in 1997 as Volkswagen, the market leader and price setter, increases the local content of its cars, thus cutting costs.

"In 1997, our Santana model will achieve 95 percent local content and Santana 2000 85 percent," said Posth. The company's other models will also boost their portion of low-cost locally made parts to 90 percent for the Jetta and 65 percent for the Audi 2000, he said.
